articles.title: Resolving melanoma heterogeneity at single-cell resolution: implications for target discovery and therapy resistance.
articles.abstract: Melanoma is characterized by profound intra-tumoural heterogeneity and a complex tumour microenvironment (TME), which are primary drivers of therapy resistance. Conventional bulk sequencing lacks the resolution to capture these cellular nuances. Single-cell technologies, particularly single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) and spatial multiomics, have fundamentally advanced our understanding of melanoma by enabling high-resolution characterization of malignant cell states, immune ecosystems and tumour microenvironment interactions. In this review, we summarize recent advances in single-cell multiomics studies of melanoma heterogeneity and therapy resistance, focusing on the identification of drug-tolerant persister states, immune escape mechanisms and resistance-associated cellular transitions. We further discuss how single-cell approaches facilitate target discovery, biomarker development and the rational design of combination therapies. By integrating multiomics profiling, computational modelling and pharmacological validation, these technologies provide a framework for translating cellular-level insights into precision therapeutic strategies. Finally, we highlight current challenges and future opportunities for clinical implementation of single-cell-guided approaches in refractory melanoma.

articles.title: Advanced platinum strategies for triple-negative breast cancer.
articles.abstract: Triple-negative breast cancer (TNBC) is an aggressive cancer subtype with limited treatment options. Platinum chemotherapy is incorporated into several therapeutic strategies, but its clinical benefit is constrained by resistance, toxicity, and suboptimal patient stratification. Platinum-induced DNA crosslinking remains the principal mechanism underlying antitumor activity. Recent studies indicate that Pt(IV) prodrugs, multifunctional agents, subcellularly targeted complexes, and tumor-responsive delivery systems can extend platinum pharmacology beyond conventional cytotoxicity. In parallel, studies have revealed emerging vulnerabilities, including homologous recombination deficiency, immunogenic cell death, ferroptosis, and DNA damage response dependencies, that provide new opportunities to enhance efficacy and overcome resistance. Advanced translational models and biomarker-guided stratification may help translate these opportunities into more precise therapeutic strategies. In this article, we review these developments and discuss their implications for advanced platinum therapies in TNBC.

articles.title: From NAD+ elevation to clinical benefit: tissue-specific regulation and translational barriers in aging and age-related disease.
articles.abstract: Nicotinamide adenine dinucleotide (NAD+) decline has been implicated in aging and age-related disease, and precursor supplementation with nicotinamide riboside (NR) or nicotinamide mononucleotide (NMN) has shown efficacy in preclinical models. Human trials, however, have produced inconsistent functional outcomes, and the sources of this translational gap remain poorly defined. We combined a bibliometric analysis of 3,271 aging-focused NAD+ publications (2004-2025) with a critical synthesis of mechanistic and clinical evidence to localize where and why preclinical findings fail to translate. The bibliometric analysis revealed three structural features of the literature: (i) original research articles dominated the corpus, whereas the document-type classification cannot distinguish preclinical experiments from human observational or interventional studies; (ii) research is siloed across disease domains with limited cross-tissue comparison; and (iii) intervention-oriented keywords (NMN, NR, supplementation, drug delivery) have outpaced empirical clinical validation. Mechanistic synthesis showed that these structural gaps correspond to biological heterogeneity: NAD+ biosynthesis, consumption, redox balance, and subcellular compartmentalization are tissue- and compartment-specific, such that systemic precursor elevation does not uniformly restore functional NAD+ in disease-relevant tissues. Four subcellular pools-nuclear, cytosolic, mitochondrial, and axonal-each possess distinct rate-limiting bottlenecks, and hepatic metabolic reserve introduces an overlooked source of inter-individual variability. Across neurodegeneration, metabolic disease, cardiovascular aging, and sarcopenia, NAD+ dysregulation follows disease-specific mechanisms rather than a universal decline phenotype. We propose a precision-medicine framework that shifts the core question from whether NAD+ can be elevated to whether a defined intervention corrects a specific NAD+ defect in the appropriate tissue and subcellular compartment. This framework provides a structured basis for designing next-generation NAD+-targeted trials with tissue-specific biomarkers and function-oriented endpoints.

articles.title: Phytocannabinoids in neurologic, neuropsychiatric, inflammatory, pain, cardiometabolic, hepatic, renal, and neoplastic disorders: Pharmacology, clinical evidence, and translational perspectives.
articles.abstract: Phytocannabinoids are pharmacologically diverse constituents of Cannabis sativa whose actions go beyond canonical cannabinoid receptors. Δ9-Tetrahydrocannabinol (THC) and cannabidiol (CBD) are best characterized, while cannabigerol, cannabidivarin, tetrahydrocannabivarin, cannabichromene, cannabinol, and related compounds are emerging candidates. This review integrates molecular pharmacology, pharmacokinetics, safety, and therapeutic evidence across neurologic, neuropsychiatric, inflammatory, pain, cardiovascular and metabolic, hepatic, renal, and neoplastic disorders. The strongest evidence supports pharmaceutical-grade oral CBD as adjunctive therapy for seizures associated with Dravet syndrome, Lennox-Gastaut syndrome, and tuberous sclerosis complex, and standardized THC-CBD formulations for selected patients with multiple sclerosis-associated spasticity. Emerging clinical signals in schizophrenia, pain, fibromyalgia, sleep disturbance, substance-use disorders, dermatologic conditions, sickle cell disease, and other symptom-focused indications support continued development. However, efficacy remains compound-, formulation-, exposure-, and indication-specific. In oncology, supportive-care applications must remain distinct from tumor-directed treatment, for which clinical efficacy has not been established. Preclinical studies show coherent effects on neuronal excitability, glial and immune activation, endothelial dysfunction, oxidative and nitrative stress, mitochondrial injury, fibrosis, and regulated cell death. These findings support further investigation in neurodegeneration, ischemia-reperfusion injury, diabetic cardiovascular disease, immune-mediated disorders, hepatic and renal injury, and selected cancers. Translation is constrained by product heterogeneity, variable exposure, uncertain target engagement, model differences, drug interactions, and underpowered trials. Standardized products, exposure-informed dosing, pharmacodynamic biomarkers, responder-enriched designs, and indication-specific randomized studies can address these barriers. Phytocannabinoids therefore represent a promising therapeutic platform whose potential will be best realized by matching defined compounds and formulations to biologically coherent diseases, mechanisms, treatment windows, and patient populations.

articles.title: Exploring the medicine-food potential of cucurbitacins: From phytochemistry, biosynthesis and structure-activity relationships to translational perspectives.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Cucurbitacins are a class of highly oxidized triterpenoid compounds widely distributed in medicinal and edible plants, exhibiting significant phytochemical diversity and broad-spectrum preclinical potential in chronic disease therapy. However, current studies mainly focus on the in vitro pharmacological effects of individual compounds, whereas a comprehensive understanding of their structural basis, bioactivity, human exposure safety, and translational feasibility remains insufficient. PURPOSE: This review aims to summarize recent advances in cucurbitacin phytochemistry, biosynthesis and structure-activity relationships (SAR), thereby providing perspectives for biomedical and dietary translation. METHODS: The relationships between structural diversity and functional complexity were analyzed, with particular emphasis on their regulatory effects in chronic disease-associated processes, including inflammation, hepatic disorders, cancer progression, and metabolic dysfunction. Emerging strategies for overcoming translational barriers were also discussed. RESULTS: Cucurbitacins exert diverse biological effects through the modulation of multiple signaling pathways and metabolic networks. Their unique structural features serve as the foundation for both beneficial effects and potential limitations, including intrinsic toxicity and extremely restricted clinical applications. Current challenges involving safety evaluation, clinical validation, and regulatory frameworks are discussed. Future strategies integrating artificial intelligence-assisted design, SAR-guided molecular optimization, and targeted delivery technologies may facilitate the development of cucurbitacins as functional bioactive ingredients with medicine-food applications. CONCLUSION: Cucurbitacin is an important medicinal resource in traditional medicine with potential for therapeutic and functional applications. Future multidisciplinary efforts integrating structural optimization, biosynthetic engineering, delivery technologies, and regulatory considerations will be essential for balancing efficacy, safety, and sensory quality, thereby supporting their rational development and further evaluation of their broader applications in food and biomedical fields.

articles.title: Triptonide alleviates sepsis-associated acute lung injury by suppressing the STAT3/HIF-1α-mediated aerobic glycolysis in macrophages.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Sepsis-associated acute lung injury (SA-ALI), represents a major contributor to mortality among septic patients during the early hyperinflammatory phase. Triptonide, a diterpenoids extract from Tripterygium wilfordii Hook f has anticancer and contraceptive effects. However, its potential and mechanism in SA-ALI are largely unknown. This study aims to evaluate the therapeutic efficacy and elucidate underlying mechanisms of triptonide in SA-ALI to identify new clinical strategies. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Lipopolysaccharide (LPS)-induced endotoxemia model or caecal ligation and puncture (CLP) model was used to induce SA-ALI in mice, accompanied by treatment with triptonide, triptolide and 2-methoxyestradiol. Parallel in vitro experiments involved LPS-treated mouse primary macrophages cultured with or without triptonide. Transcriptomic sequencing of macrophages was performed to explore the anti-inflammatory mechanisms of triptonide, which were further substantiated using specific activators, inhibitors and adeno-associated virus (AAV)-mediated gene targeting. KEY RESULTS: Our data shows that triptonide effectively inhibits macrophage pro-inflammatory activation, reduces pulmonary inflammation and alleviates SA-ALI pathology (i.e. inflammatory cell infiltration, oedema and cell apoptosis), thereby improving the survival of septic mice. Transcriptomic sequencing combined with metabolic analysis shows that triptonide suppresses aerobic glycolysis in pro-inflammatory macrophages by inhibiting the Signal Transducer and Activator of Transcription 3 (STAT3)/Hypoxia inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α) axis. Notably, the therapeutic efficacy of triptonide against SA-ALI was abolished in myeloid cell-specific HIF-1α overexpressed mice (LyzM-CreDIO-hif1a mice). CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: Triptonide protects against SA-ALI by suppressing the STAT3/HIF-1α signalling axis, thereby inhibiting aerobic glycolysis-mediated pro-inflammatory macrophage activation, which suggests that triptonide is a promising therapeutic strategy for SA-ALI.

articles.title: Impact of Food and Beverage on Enlicitide Pharmacokinetics and LDL-C Lowering.
articles.abstract: Enlicitide decanoate is a macrocyclic peptide first-in-class oral PCSK9 inhibitor that lowers LDL-C, with maximal efficacy achieved when administered on an empty stomach. This work characterizes the effects of food, pre-dose fasting duration (2-8 hours), water volume, common beverages (black coffee and plain tea), and other real-world scenarios on enlicitide exposure and predicts the impact on clinical efficacy. Three phase I, open-label, crossover studies in healthy participants evaluated the effects of these conditions on enlicitide exposure following a single 20 mg dose. Enlicitide steady-state exposure and corresponding LDL-C reductions under various conditions were predicted using population pharmacokinetic and exposure-response models. Administration of enlicitide 30 minutes after a high-fat meal resulted in an approximately 48% reduction in steady-state AUC and delayed absorption compared with fasted conditions (median Tmax ~8 hours vs. 0.5-1 hour). Increasing pre-dose fasting duration from 2 to 8 hours increased exposure. Water volume, black coffee or plain tea had no meaningful effect on enlicitide exposure. Model-predicted LDL-C reductions remained robust across various conditions, with LDL-C reductions of approximately 64% under fasted conditions, 62% to 63% when occasionally administered with food or if a dose is occasionally missed, 60% with black coffee or plain tea, and 59% following a 4-hour fast. These data support the recommended dosing and administration instructions for enlicitide, which are expected to provide ~60% LDL-C reduction, as seen in the enlicitide phase III clinical trials. Furthermore, these findings highlight the pharmacokinetic forgiveness potential of enlicitide, suggesting that occasional departures from the recommended dosing or sporadic lapses in compliance may be tolerated with minimal impact on efficacy.

articles.title: An inhibitor of the mitochondrial respiratory chain exerts synergistic anti-tumour effects when combined with alkylating agents.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Cancer cells exhibit the Warburg effect, but oxidative phosphorylation (OXPHOS) is also important for cancer cell proliferation. Metabolic reprogramming from glycolysis to OXPHOS is one mechanism of resistance to anti-tumour drugs. Here, we have synthesized and characterized OPB-111077, a novel, first-in-class orally available small-molecule compound, and investigated its anti-tumour activity and therapeutic potential in combination with alkylating agents. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Inhibition of mitochondrial function by OPB-111077 were assessed by measuring the oxygen consumption rate, ATP production and Complex I enzymatic activity. anti-tumour effects were evaluated in human haematological and solid tumour cell lines and in cell line-derived xenograft and lymphoma patient-derived xenograft models. Mechanistic studies included CRISPR screening, metabolomic analyses, and measurements of the oxygen consumption and extracellular acidification rates. Effects of OPB-111077 combined with alkylating agents were also assessed in mice. KEY RESULTS: OPB-111077 inhibited mitochondrial respiratory chain Complex I, suppressed OXPHOS, and exerted anti-tumour effects in several models. OPB-111077 demonstrated synergism with the alkylating agent bendamustine, with simultaneous inhibition of both OXPHOS and glycolysis. Bendamustine reprogrammed cancer cells into an OXPHOS-dominant state, thereby enhancing the efficacy of OPB-111077. CONCLUSION AND IMPLICATIONS: Based on these findings, we propose a novel anticancer therapeutic strategy of combining OXPHOS inhibitors with alkylating agents. OPB-111077 has demonstrated potential in combination therapy and was recently evaluated with bendamustine and rituximab in a Phase 1 clinical trial for patients with relapsed/refractory diffuse large B-cell lymphoma (NCT04049825).

articles.title: Patient-anchored pharmacological modeling prioritizes combined miR-4651/miR-6126 for experimental validation in Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome.
articles.abstract: Hutchinson-Gilford progeria syndrome (HGPS) is characterized by accelerated vascular aging, but therapeutic development is constrained by sparse longitudinal clinical data and the limited number of independent biological models. We developed a patient-anchored framework integrating longitudinal cardiovascular phenotyping, endothelial transcriptomics, LMNA cryptic splicing, biological-line-preserving virtual populations, treatment counterfactuals and lipid nanoparticle (LNP) delivery optimization. The index patient showed progressive carotid disease and worsening diastolic indices despite preserved systolic function. In HGPS endothelial cells, disease-associated transcriptional structure persisted after adjustment for cell-cycle and flow-related effects across 20,404 non-cell-cycle genes (Spearman ρ = 0.706), with inflammatory activation remaining directionally positive in all five leave-one-line-out refits. Hierarchical modeling generated 2,000 virtual profiles per condition for uncertainty propagation without increasing biological sample size or statistical power. Under the prespecified treatment operators, patient-informed counterfactual simulations ranked combined miR-4651/miR-6126 above either single agent across 6-, 12- and 24-month horizons; however, a separate uncalibrated structural sensitivity model showed that dual-treatment superiority was not robust to matched total miRNA cargo and hypothetical competitive or antagonistic interactions. A four-dimensional computational LNP optimization screen evaluated 18,072 regimens, retained 2,567 Pareto-nondominated solutions and narrowed these to 30 model-prioritized delivery configurations for experimental evaluation. Together, these analyses connect observed HGPS vascular pathology with biologically constrained therapeutic prioritization, identify combined miR-4651/miR-6126 as a model-prioritized candidate requiring matched-dose experimental validation, rather than an intervention with established superiority, and define a model-prioritized LNP delivery space for HGPS vascular disease.

articles.title: Targeting the FKBP5-ceramide axis driven mitochondrial reprogramming in cardiac macrophages attenuates post-infarct cardiac injury.
articles.abstract: Plasma ceramide levels are elevated in cardiovascular disease and predict recurrent adverse events and mortality after myocardial infarction (MI). However, mechanisms driving post-MI ceramide accumulation and pharmacologically actionable targets to counteract ceramide-driven myocardial damage are still lacking. Here, we identify FK506-binding protein 5 (FKBP5) as a druggable immunometabolic regulator of ceramide metabolism in cardiac macrophages, linking FKBP5 suppression to interrupted pathological crosstalk among sphingolipid remodeling, mitochondrial impairment and post-MI inflammatory injury. Using murine MI models and FKBP5-deficient cells, we examined FKBP5 inhibition or deficiency reduced infarct size and fibrosis, improved cardiac function, and protected against adverse remodeling. Mechanistically, FKBP5 was associated with the sphingomyelin phosphodiesterase 3 (Smpd3) promoter region and contributed to the regulation of its transcriptional activity after MI, thereby promoting ceramide accumulation. Specifically, FKBP5-mediated ceramide 24:1 (Cer24:1) upregulation impaired mitochondrial redox homeostasis by disrupting electron transport chain integrity, thereby reinforcing M1 polarization and exacerbating myocardial injury. Elevated Cer24:1 directly bound the mitochondrial TU translation elongation factor (TUFM), disrupting electron transport chain integrity and mitochondrial respiration, providing a defined link between ceramide species and mitochondrial dysfunction. Notably, in vivo treatment with Cer24:1 attenuated the cardioprotective effects of FKBP5 inhibition after MI. Collectively, we describe a previously unrecognized FKBP5-Smpd3-Cer24:1-TUFM signaling axis in cardiac macrophages. FKBP5-governed ceramide metabolism drives macrophage immunometabolic reprogramming, marking FKBP5 as a promising pharmacological target for ischemic heart disease. Our findings support the role of the FKBP5-ceramide axis in mediating post-infarct myocardial dysfunction and highlight pharmacological FKBP5 inhibition as a therapeutic strategy against post-MI cardiac injury.

articles.title: Puerarin preserves microglial homeostasis and protects against acute cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury by regulating autophagy and oxidative stress through Janus kinase 2/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Microglial oxidative stress and dysregulated autophagy contribute to secondary neuronal injury following ischemic stroke. Puerarin (PUE), a bioactive isoflavone with established antioxidative and neuroprotective properties, may protect against cerebral ischemia by modulating microglial dysfunction; however, the underlying mechanisms remain unclear. METHODS: The neuroprotective effects of PUE were investigated in a rat transient middle cerebral artery occlusion (tMCAO) model and in BV2 microglia subjected to oxygen-glucose deprivation/reoxygenation (OGD/R). Microglial phenotypic alterations, oxidative stress, and autophagic activity were evaluated using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq), ultrastructural, biochemical, and fluorescence-based analyzes. Data-independent acquisition (DIA) proteomics, pharmacological gain- and loss-of-function approaches, and adeno-associated virus serotype 9 (AAV9)-mediated Janus kinase 2 (JAK2) knockdown were employed to define the role of Janus kinase 2/signal transducer and activator of transcription 3 (JAK2/STAT3) signaling. Microglia-mediated neuroprotection was further assessed using an HT22 neuron-microglia co-culture system. RESULTS: PUE reshaped the microglial landscape by preserving the homeostatic microglial phenotype while suppressing ischemia-induced pathological activation. PUE reduced intracellular and mitochondrial ROS production, restored redox homeostasis, suppressed excessive autophagosome formation, and downregulated the autophagy-related proteins 3/5/12 (ATG3/5/12). Mechanistically, these protective effects were mediated through inhibition of JAK2/STAT3 signaling. Genetic silencing of JAK2 recapitulated the effects of PUE, whereas pharmacological activation of JAK2/STAT3 largely abolished its antioxidative, anti-autophagic, and neuroprotective activities. Furthermore, conditioned media from PUE-treated microglia significantly alleviated neuronal injury in HT22 cells, supporting a microglia-mediated paracrine mechanism of neuroprotection. CONCLUSION: Collectively, these findings identify JAK2/STAT3-dependent regulation of the oxidative stress-autophagy axis as a critical mechanism underlying microglial homeostasis after acute cerebral ischemia-reperfusion injury (CIRI) and establish PUE as a promising therapeutic candidate for ischemic stroke.

articles.title: Activity of the natural biflavonoid hinokiflavone against multidrug-resistant CEM/ADR5000 leukemia cells and its modes of action via P-glycoprotein modulation.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Multidrug resistance (MDR), frequently associated with the overexpression of ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporters such as P-glycoprotein (P-gp), is a major obstacle to successful leukemia chemotherapy. Natural products represent an important source for anticancer drug discovery. Hinokiflavone, a natural biflavonoid, has demonstrated anticancer potential, but its underlying mechanisms against multidrug-resistant leukemia are largely unknown. HYPOTHESIS: We hypothesized that hinokiflavone exhibits preferential activity against P-gp-overexpressing multidrug-resistant leukemia cells through specific mechanisms associated with the multidrug-resistant phenotype. METHODS: Cytotoxicity was evaluated in parental and drug-resistant cell models, and the contribution of ABCB1/P-gp to the collateral sensitivity of CEM/ADR5000 cells was investigated by siRNA-mediated ABCB1 knockdown. Molecular docking was performed to predict potential interactions with both P-gp and breast cancer resistance protein (BCRP). mRNA-based transcriptomic expression profiling, Western blot analysis, pathway analyses, and siRNA-mediated TXNIP knockdown were used to investigate signaling alterations. Intracellular ROS generation, mitochondrial membrane potential, P-gp-associated drug transport, ATP levels, cell cycle distribution, DNA damage, and apoptosis were further investigated. In addition, a zebrafish xenograft model was used to evaluate preliminary in vivo antitumor activity. RESULTS: Hinokiflavone exhibited collateral sensitivity toward P-gp-overexpressing CEM/ADR5000 leukemia cells, and ABCB1 knockdown markedly reduced this sensitivity. Moreover, hinokiflavone significantly restored doxorubicin sensitivity in multidrug-resistant CEM/ADR5000 cells, reducing the IC₅₀ of doxorubicin by 3.17-fold, comparable to the P-glycoprotein inhibitor verapamil. Molecular docking predicted interactions with both P-gp and BCRP. Transcriptomic and protein analyses revealed alterations in several signaling pathways (activated WNT/β-catenin signaling, increased TXNIP and PTEN expression, and reduced PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling). TXNIP knockdown attenuated the effects of hinokiflavone on PI3K/AKT/mTOR signaling and reduced the cytotoxic response. Hinokiflavone treatment was also associated with ROS accumulation, mitochondrial membrane depolarization, altered P-gp-associated drug transport, ATP depletion, G2/M-related cell-cycle alterations, DNA damage, and apoptosis. Hinokiflavone additionally exhibited preliminary antitumor activity in an SK-N-DZ zebrafish xenograft model. CONCLUSION: Hinokiflavone exhibits collateral sensitivity in P-gp-overexpressing CEM/ADR5000 leukemia cells, with ABCB1/P-glycoprotein contributing substantially to this phenotype. Its activity is associated with oxidative stress, energy metabolism, P-gp-associated drug transport, and multiple survival signaling pathways. These findings highlight hinokiflavone's potential for targeting multidrug-resistant leukemia.

articles.title: TSP promotes ferroptosis in breast cancer cells to suppress osteolytic bone metastasis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Tiaowei Shenqi pill (TSP) is clinically applied for the treatment of osteoporosis and breast cancer (BC). This study aims to explore the effects and mechanisms of TSP in bone metastasis during BC. METHODS: An experimental bone colonization model was established in BALB/c mice by injecting 4T1.2 cells into the left ventricle to evaluate BC cell bone metastasis and osteolytic bone destruction. A BC orthotopic tumor model was established by administering MDA-MB-231 cells into the fat pad of BALB/c nude mice. BC cells were co-cultured with osteoblasts MC3T3-E1 for an in vitro study. RESULTS: TSP inhibited orthotopic tumor growth and enhanced ferroptosis-related phenotypes, accompanied by downregulation of SREBF1, upregulation of RASSF1, increased phosphorylation of YAP1 at Ser127, and reduced YAP1 nuclear localization. TSP-containing serum (TSP-CS) reduced the response of BC cells to migration-promoting signals from osteoblast-conditioned medium. TSP treatment also reduced tumor burden in bone metastases, accompanied by a decrease in osteoblast-associated markers around cancer cells. Overexpression of SREBF1 suppressed RASSF1 expression, reduced YAP1 phosphorylation at Ser127, and promoted YAP1 nuclear localization. SREBF1 overexpression reversed TSP-induced ferroptosis and the suppression of bone metastasis and intrabone tumor burden, whereas subsequent RASSF1 overexpression could partially rescue these phenotypes. The YAP activator PY-60 further reversed the enhanced ferroptosis induced by RASSF1. CONCLUSIONS: TSP downregulates SREBF1 expression; this change is associated with increased RASSF1 transcription and is accompanied by reduced nuclear localization of YAP1. The findings of this study support the hypothesis that the SREBF1/RASSF1/YAP1 axis may be involved in TSP-induced ferroptosis in BC cells.

articles.title: Ginkgolide K restrains pulmonary fibrosis by disrupting a STING-FTH1 proteolytic ferroptosis axis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is driven by persistent fibroblast activation and excessive extracellular matrix deposition. Stimulator of interferon genes (STING) has been implicated in tissue fibrosis, but whether it directly regulates ferroptosis and iron homeostasis in fibroblasts through noncanonical mechanisms remains unclear. Ginkgolide K (GinK), a bioactive diterpene trilactone from Ginkgo biloba, has antioxidant and immunomodulatory properties, but its role in PF is poorly understood. PURPOSE: This study aimed to define the role of STING in ferroptosis-associated fibroblast activation and to determine whether GinK exerts antifibrotic effects by targeting this pathway. STUDY DESIGN AND METHODS: Bleomycin-induced PF was established in wild-type and STING-knockout mice, and TGF-β1-stimulated NIH/3T3 fibroblasts were used as an in vitro model. STING gain- and loss-of-function approaches were used to determine its role in fibroblast activation and ferroptosis. IP-MS, co-immunoprecipitation, ubiquitination assays, cycloheximide chase, and proteasome inhibition were performed to investigate the regulation of ferritin heavy chain 1 (FTH1) stability. Ferroptosis-associated changes were assessed by measuring intracellular Fe²⁺, lipid peroxidation, and related protein markers. Representative ginkgolide constituents were subsequently screened, and the pharmacological effects of GinK were evaluated in vitro and in vivo. Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) and experiments using a STING triple mutant were performed to examine GinK-STING binding and STING involvement in the cellular response to GinK. RESULTS: STING expression was increased in fibrotic lungs and activated fibroblasts. STING knockout attenuated BLM-induced pulmonary fibrosis, and STING silencing reduced fibroblast activation. STING promoted intracellular Fe²⁺ accumulation and lipid peroxidation, linking STING activation to ferroptotic stress. Mechanistically, STING associated with FTH1 and promoted its polyubiquitination and proteasome-dependent degradation without altering Fth1 mRNA levels. Loss of FTH1 disrupted iron homeostasis and enhanced ferroptosis-associated fibroblast activation. This effect was not reproduced by cGAMP stimulation and was not prevented by cGAS inhibition, supporting a noncanonical STING mechanism independent of upstream cGAS-cGAMP activation. Integrated proteomic and ubiquitination analyses further identified NEDD4 as a candidate E3 ligase involved in FTH1 turnover. Among the ginkgolide constituents screened, GinK showed the strongest predicted interaction with STING. GinK suppressed STING abundance, restored FTH1-mediated iron homeostasis, reduced ferroptotic stress and fibroblast activation, and attenuated bleomycin-induced PF. STING overexpression markedly weakened the protective effects of GinK. SPR demonstrated GinK-STING binding with a steady-state KD of 12.48 μM. GinK did not significantly reduce intracellular Fe²⁺ accumulation or lipid peroxidation in cells expressing the S161A/R237A/T262A STING mutant under the tested conditions. CONCLUSION: GinK alleviates pulmonary fibrosis by suppressing a noncanonical STING-FTH1 pathway that promotes FTH1 degradation, iron dyshomeostasis, and ferroptosis-associated fibroblast activation. These findings support a mechanism linking STING to fibroblast ferroptosis and provide a mechanistic basis for the antifibrotic activity of GinK.

articles.title: Rhein suppresses prostate cancer growth in vitro and in vivo by inducing apoptosis and ferroptosis.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Prostate cancer (PCa) is one of the most common malignancies in men worldwide. Conventional treatments face limitations including drug resistance, metastasis, and adverse effects. Rhein, an 1,8-dihydroxyanthraquinone derived from Rheum palmatum, exhibits anti-inflammatory and anti-tumor activities. However, its therapeutic potential against PCa and its ability to simultaneously induce multiple programmed cell death pathways remain unclear. OBJECTIVE: To systematically investigate the anti-tumor effects of rhein on PCa cells in vitro and in vivo, and elucidate the molecular mechanisms, with a focus on whether rhein induces both apoptosis and ferroptosis. METHODS: The anti-proliferative effects of rhein on PCa cells (PC-3 and DU-145) were assessed using CCK-8, EdU incorporation, colony formation, and live/dead staining. Cell migration and EMT-related proteins were evaluated by wound healing, Transwell, and Western blot. Network pharmacology and transcriptomics were used to predict the potential mechanisms. Flow cytometry served to determine cell cycle distribution and apoptosis rate. Ferroptosis was evaluated by measuring ROS, Fe2+, MDA levels, along with C11-BODIPY staining, GSH quantification, and transmission electron microscopy (TEM) analysis, with rescue experiments using ferroptosis inhibitors. Pathway involvement was validated through MAPK agonist/inhibitor assays and p53 siRNA knockdown targeting the SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway. A DU-145 xenograft model was established to assess the in vivo anti-tumor activity and systemic toxicity of rhein. RESULTS: Rhein inhibited PCa cell proliferation, migration, and EMT, arrested the cell cycle at S phase, and significantly induced apoptosis. Rhein treatment increased ROS, Fe2+, and MDA levels, depleted GSH, and induced lipid peroxidation and mitochondrial morphological changes typical of ferroptosis, the biochemical markers of ferroptosis were reversed by ferroptosis inhibitor, confirming the specificity of rhein-induced ferroptosis. Mechanistically, MAPK pathway agonists reversed rhein-induced apoptosis, while p53 knockdown attenuated rhein-induced SLC7A11/GPX4 downregulation, confirming that rhein acts through MAPK suppression and the p53/SLC7A11/GPX4 axis. In vivo, rhein significantly inhibited DU-145 xenograft growth, reduced the expression of GPX4, SLC7A11, and Ki-67 in tumor tissues, and showed no significant toxicity to the liver and kidney. CONCLUSION: Rhein effectively inhibits PCa growth in vitro and in vivo by inducing S-phase arrest, promoting apoptosis (via MAPK pathway), and inducing ferroptosis (via p53/SLC7A11/GPX4 pathway), with low systemic toxicity. Unlike previous studies focusing on a single death pathway, this work demonstrates that rhein simultaneously induces apoptosis and ferroptosis in PCa via complementary MAPK and p53/SLC7A11/GPX4 mechanisms, supporting natural product-based multi-mechanistic strategies for cancer therapy.

articles.title: Multiscale and cross-organ antidiabetic effects of Ajuga decumbens and harpagide: Integrating hepatic metabolism, immune regulation, and gut microbiota.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) is a complex metabolic disorder involving dysregulated glucose homeostasis and interconnected disturbances across multiple organs. Plant-derived bioactive compounds represent promising candidates for metabolic regulation. Although Ajuga decumbens exhibits anti-inflammatory and lipid-modulating activities, its antidiabetic potential and underlying mechanisms remain insufficiently characterized, particularly from a multiscale and cross-organ perspective. PURPOSE: This exploratory study aimed to evaluate the antidiabetic activities of A. decumbens extracts, identify candidate bioactive constituents, and investigate their potential mechanisms within an integrated multiscale framework. METHODS: An integrated experimental strategy combining in vivo, in vitro, in silico, and omics-based approaches was employed. High-fat diet (HFD)-fed diabetic mice were used to evaluate acute and long-term metabolic effects. α-amylase inhibition assays were performed to investigate potential effects on carbohydrate digestion. Phytochemical profiling, quantitative chromatography, molecular docking, and molecular dynamics simulations were conducted to identify and characterize candidate bioactive constituents. Transcriptomic analysis and 16S rRNA gene sequencing were used to explore hepatic molecular responses and gut microbial alterations. Integrated correlation network analysis was subsequently performed to examine associations among metabolic phenotypes, hepatic gluconeogenic signaling, immune polarization, and gut microbiota. RESULTS: Ajuga decumbens leaf extract (ALE) reduced postprandial blood glucose by 27.77% following an acute starch challenge and inhibited α-amylase activity (IC₅₀ = 47.39 ± 8.84 μg/ml). Harpagide (HPG), identified as a quantitatively prominent bioactive constituent, also exhibited α-amylase inhibitory activity (IC₅₀ = 8.01 ± 1.48 μg/ml) and reduced postprandial glucose by 25.99%. Four weeks of treatment improved glycemic regulation, lipid metabolism, and insulin resistance-related indices while attenuating diabetes-associated histopathological abnormalities. Mechanistic investigations indicated that ALE and HPG modulated hepatic gluconeogenesis-associated signaling through the Akt/FoxO1 pathway and altered macrophage polarization-related markers. Both treatments were also associated with changes in gut microbial composition, including the relative abundances of an uncultured taxon within Desulfobacterota, Colidextribacter, and the Eubacterium xylanophilum group. Integrated correlation analysis further revealed two partially differentiated association networks linking hepatic gluconeogenic regulation, immune polarization, gut microbial composition and diversity, and metabolic phenotypes. CONCLUSION: These findings provide integrated evidence supporting the antidiabetic potential of A. decumbens leaf extract and HPG through multiple biological processes involving intestinal α-amylase inhibition, hepatic gluconeogenic regulation, immune modulation, and gut microbial alterations. The identification of distinct cross-scale association patterns provides a systematic framework for investigating their metabolic effects and supports further mechanistic and preclinical evaluation of ALE and HPG as plant-derived candidates for T2DM management.

articles.title: Emerging antibody-drug conjugate (ADC) therapies: perspectives from the global patent landscape.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs) represent one of the most significant innovations in biopharmaceutical research, integrating antibody target specificity with the cytotoxic potency of small-molecule payloads. Despite rapid progress, the technological structure and knowledge dynamics underlying ADC innovation remain insufficiently characterized. This study aimed to map the ADC technological landscape through patent analysis of 6,620 patent families published before 30 June 2025. METHOD: BERTopic was applied to extract global topics, and characterize the ADC knowledge structure. A directed patent citation network was constructed at the patent family level, and patent citations were aggregated by dominant topic to establish a topic citation network. Degree-based and PageRank metrics were used to identify key topics and evaluate their functional roles in knowledge flow. RESULTS: The analysis categorized 47 technological topics into nine clusters covering Target Selection, Biological Mechanisms, Antibody Structure, Therapeutic Indications, Conjugation Chemistry, Linker Chemistry, Payload Modality, Delivery Systems, Formulations and Stability. Ten key topics were identified as hubs within the topic citation network, comprising five target topics: B-cell surface antigens, B7 family antigens, Mesothelin, AXL, and HER family receptors; two payload topics: PBD payloads and Camptothecin-derived payloads; two mechanism topics: Interleukin immunocytokine and Immune checkpoint modulation, and one delivery topic: Nanoparticle delivery. Topic role analysis indicated distinct patterns among absorption-oriented, diffusion-oriented, and bridging topics in shaping knowledge absorption, dissemination, and trans-topic reorganization. CONCLUSION: This study provides an evidence-based view of the ADC patent landscape and offers strategic insights for target prioritization, payload design, and R&D planning. It also demonstrates the applicability of integrated patent landscape analysis to other emerging technology fields.

articles.title: I Have a Medical Degree. Should I Consider a Career in Clinical Pharmacology in 2026?
Pharmacological targeting of phosphodiesterase-5 halts pulmonary fibrosis by suppressing epithelial-mesenchymal transition via cGMP/PKG/Smad/HDAC2 pathway.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND AND PURPOSE: Pulmonary fibrosis (PF) is a progressive and incurable disease with activation of epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) as a crucial pathological step. Despite advances in elucidating its pathogenesis, therapeutic options for PF remain very limited. Although raising intracellular levels of cGMP mitigated fibrosis in animal models, the mechanism(s) underlying this action, particularly concerning EMT, remain unclear. PDE5, a key cGMP-hydrolyzing enzyme, is a promising therapeutic target, as some PDE5 inhibitors are in clinical use. EXPERIMENTAL APPROACH: Two well-established rat models of PF, induced by bleomycin or paraquat were used to elucidate the therapeutic potential and mechanisms underpinning effects of the PDE5 inhibitor tadalafil on pulmonary fibrogenesis. KEY RESULTS: Daily administration of tadalafil attenuated PF development and lung injury. even when administered at an advanced stage of PF, tadalafil significantly attenuated fibrotic progression and improved lung histopathology. Mechanistically, tadalafil exerted its therapeutic effect by suppressing the canonical TGF-β/Smad signaling pathway and EMT through a cGMP/PKG pathway. Immunohistochemical and immunofluorescence analyses corroborated the in‑vivo antifibrotic activity of tadalafil. Preliminary results indicated PKG‑dependent down-regulation of histone deacetylase 2 (HDAC2) expression and elevated acetylated histones. Knockdown and pharmacological inhibition of HDAC2 mimicked effects of tadalafil, whereas over-expression of HDAC2 negated tadalafil's effects on EMT, implying a key mechanistic role for HDAC2. CONCLUSIONS AND IMPLICATIONS: Tadalafil halted progression of PF by inhibiting EMT, most likely through a PKG-mediated pathway counteracting TGF-β-induced HDAC2 expression. Our findings, together with the well-tolerated safety profile. warrant immediate clinical assessment of repurposing tadalafil for the treatment of pulmonary fibrosis.

articles.title: Angiotensin receptor blockers and nontraditional health outcomes: an umbrella review of meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials.
articles.abstract: AIM: Angiotensin receptor blockers (ARBs) are prescribed for cardiovascular and renal protection, but their effects on nontraditional health outcomes remain unclear. With the increasing use of ARBs in diverse populations, clarifying their broader impact has important clinical implications. METHODS: We conducted an umbrella review of systematic reviews and meta-analyses of randomised controlled trials (RCTs) that assessed ARBs and nontraditional health outcomes. PubMed, Embase, Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from inception to April 2026. Methodological quality was appraised using AMSTAR 2, and certainty of evidence was assessed using GRADE. Where trial-level data were available, we re-analysed outcomes using random-effects models and evaluated heterogeneity, 95% prediction intervals, and small-study effects. RESULTS: Fifteen systematic reviews and meta-analyses of RCTs were included, covering 35 unique nontraditional outcomes. Nine outcomes reached nominal statistical significance, but only a few met more stringent credibility criteria. The most credible associations were lower risks of headache and new-onset diabetes, and lower fasting plasma insulin levels with ARB therapy. Associations with migraine severity, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol, and insulin resistance were suggestive or exploratory because of prediction intervals crossing the null, sparse data, heterogeneity, or limited certainty. No convincing evidence supported associations with oncological, infectious, or transplant-related outcomes. Most included reviews were rated as low or critically low-quality using AMSTAR 2, warranting cautious interpretation. CONCLUSION: ARBs appear to provide therapeutic benefits beyond traditional indications, particularly in metabolic and neurological domains, without evidence of excess harm. These findings may inform clinical decision-making in patients at risk of diabetes or with comorbid pain conditions.

articles.title: Degraders take on GPCRs.
Targeting Stress-Adaptive States: An Emerging Framework in Cancer Pharmacology.
articles.abstract: The failure of cancer therapy is largely driven by the remarkable capacity of tumor cells to adapt to pharmacological stress. Beyond genetic alterations and signaling pathway rewiring, malignant cells exploit dynamic stress-adaptive protein states that promote survival under cytotoxic conditions. Rather than providing a descriptive summary of the emerging literature, this review offers a critical analysis of the evidence supporting these adaptive states as therapeutic vulnerabilities. We evaluate the mechanistic basis, experimental limitations, and translational potential of non-canonical drug targets, including ribosomal specialization, translational reprogramming, phase-separated biomolecular condensates, and proteostasis buffering systems. By integrating insights from translational control, protein homeostasis, and stress biology, we critically assess current pharmacological strategies aimed at disrupting adaptive buffering capacity in cancer cells and identify the key challenges that must be overcome for clinical translation. We propose that quantifying stress-adaptive cellular states, rather than focusing solely on individual oncogenic proteins, offers a complementary extension of current frameworks - including drug-tolerant persister biology, non-oncogene addiction, and phenotypic plasticity - with the potential to delay or prevent therapy resistance. This perspective broadens the concept of druggable targets and highlights stress-adaptive protein states as an underexplored frontier for the development of more durable cancer therapies.

articles.title: Ginsenosides in hepatocellular carcinoma: preclinical evidence, mechanisms, and clinical implications.
articles.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a major cause of cancer mortality worldwide, with limited effectiveness of current strategies and persistent challenges in early detection and outcome prediction. This review summarizes the preclinical evidence supporting the therapeutic potential of ginsenosides from Panax ginseng-particularly Rh2 and Rg3-in HCC cellular and animal models. Mechanistically, the antitumor effects are discussed in relation to induction of apoptosis, modulation of autophagy and other cell-death-associated signaling, and reprogramming of the tumor microenvironment, alongside evidence for suppression of metastatic behavior and enhancement of antitumor immunity. Finally, the review provides clinical implications by highlighting how these mechanistic findings may inform future translation, including opportunities for rational combination regimens and drug delivery approaches to overcome key translational bottlenecks-particularly low bioavailability and the lack of reliable biomarkers for response prediction and patient stratification-to optimize clinical application. Overall, the available preclinical data suggest that ginsenosides are promising candidates for improving HCC management, while emphasizing the need for further mechanistically rigorous and translational studies to support clinical optimization.

articles.title: Natural products target the NRF2-ferroptosis axis in hepatocellular carcinoma: tumor sensitization versus hepatoprotection.
articles.abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) remains a major cause of cancer mortality. First-line systemic therapy is now led by immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI)-based regimens, notably atezolizumab plus bevacizumab and durvalumab plus tremelimumab, whereas sorafenib and lenvatinib are used mainly when immunotherapy is unsuitable and in later lines; resistance limits the durability of both strategies. Ferroptosis, an iron-dependent form of regulated cell death driven by phospholipid peroxidation, offers a potential strategy for overcoming this resistance. Nuclear factor erythroid 2-related factor 2 (NRF2) is a central but context-dependent regulator of this vulnerability. Transient NRF2 activation protects non-transformed hepatocytes from oxidative injury, whereas constitutive activation in HCC reinforces SLC7A11-and GPX4-dependent antioxidant defenses, promotes immune escape, and supports drug resistance. This mini-review evaluates how natural products and related formulations modulate this dual program. Polyphyllin I, tiliroside, ponicidin, picropodophyllin, curcumin, esculetin, sappanone A, and decursin act at distinct upstream nodes but converge on suppression of the p62-KEAP1-NRF2 pathway or its SLC7A11/GPX4 effectors, thereby restoring ferroptotic sensitivity in preclinical HCC models. In contrast, ginsenoside Rg1, thymoquinone, and hinokitiol activate NRF2 in models of non-malignant liver injury. Because the FSP1-CoQ10 and DHODH systems defend membranes against phospholipid peroxidation independently of GPX4, residual activity in these parallel arms can limit the efficacy of agents directed at the NRF2-SLC7A11-GPX4 axis. These findings support tumor-selective NRF2 modulation rather than indiscriminate systemic inhibition. Biased disruption of the KEAP1-p62 interaction and tumor-targeted nucleic-acid delivery provide proof of concept, but translation is constrained by limited pharmacokinetic, target-engagement, toxicologic, and clinical evidence.

articles.title: Five-flavor Sophora flavescens enteric-coated capsules for ulcerative colitis: ethnopharmacological rationale, pharmacology, clinical evidence, and safety.
articles.abstract: Five-flavor Sophora flavescens enteric-coated capsules (FSEC), also reported as Wuwei Kushen or composite Sophora colon-soluble capsules, are used in China for ulcerative colitis (UC) associated with intestinal damp-heat, bloody diarrhea, and mucosal injury. This critical narrative Review evaluates the traditional rationale, product identity, material basis, pharmacological evidence, clinical findings, and safety of FSEC. PubMed, Web of Science, ScienceDirect, CNKI, Wanfang, and reference lists were searched through May 2026 and selectively updated through 18 August 2026. The Four Pillars of Best Practice in Ethnopharmacology and the ConPhyMP guidelines informed appraisal of identity, characterization, dose, and evidence attribution. The defined five-material product contains S. flavescens, Sanguisorba officinalis, Indigo naturalis, Bletilla striata, and Glycyrrhiza uralensis. Complete-formulation experiments support effects on microbial short-chain-fatty-acid signaling, GPR43, NLRP3/STAT3, AGE-RAGE/NF-κB, epithelial barrier integrity, and ferroptosis-related changes. Constituent studies broaden biological plausibility but cannot establish the efficacy or safety of the complete product. Older randomized trials and meta-analyses suggest short-term benefit, whereas recent single-center cohorts provide provisional adjunctive evidence because of nonrandomized designs and incomplete batch reporting. FSEC is therefore a plausible colon-targeted ethnopharmacological intervention, but confirmatory studies require chemically defined batches, verified release and exposure, internationally accepted UC endpoints, prospective multicenter designs, and active monitoring for hepatic, cardiopulmonary, electrolyte, and interaction risks.

articles.title: Mechanistic insights into lactate-driven pathogenesis in diabetic kidney disease.
articles.abstract: Diabetic kidney disease (DKD) remains the leading cause of end-stage renal disease worldwide, yet current therapeutic approaches fail to fully halt its progression. Emerging evidence identifies lactate not merely as a glycolytic byproduct, but as a critical signaling molecule that drives DKD pathogenesis via lysine lactylation. This review delineates the mechanistic cascade from upstream metabolic dysregulation to epigenetic reprogramming and renal injury. We first describe how the hyperglycemic and hypoxic microenvironment stabilizes hypoxia-inducible factor-1α (HIF-1α), initiating a positive feedback loop that amplifies glycolytic flux and lactate accumulation. Then, we discuss the dynamic regulation of lactylation by "writer" enzymes and "eraser" enzymes. Furthermore, we analyze how lactate-induced lactylation may contribute to metabolic and immune-inflammatory remodeling across key renal cells: promoting podocyte epithelial-mesenchymal transition (EMT) and autophagy suppression; driving tubular fibrosis and ferroptosis via specific lactylation axes; and activating glomerular endothelial NOD-like receptor family pyrin domain-containing 3 (NLRP3) inflammasomes. Beyond lactylation, we address other lactate-mediated mechanisms, including GPR81 signaling and intracellular acidification. Finally, we evaluate therapeutic strategies targeting this pathway-such as SGLT2 inhibitors and traditional Chinese medicine-and discuss the challenges in clinical translation. By integrating the latest mechanistic advances, this review discusses lactate-induced lactylation as a potential hub that may connect metabolic, epigenetic, and immune injury, while acknowledging that renal inflammation in DKD arises from diverse upstream pathways, providing a roadmap for the development of next-generation biomarkers and targeted therapies.

articles.title: Mapping the subcellular pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic landscape: a systems-pharmacology framework for predicting combination therapies against intracellular bacterial infections.
articles.abstract: Intracellular bacterial pathogens represent one of the most formidable challenges in contemporary medicine. By exploiting host cellular niches, these organisms evade immune surveillance and withstand conventional antibiotic therapies, establishing persistent reservoirs that are difficult to eradicate. Although antibiotic combinations, host-directed interventions, and drug repurposing have shown promise, conventional discovery pipelines rarely capture the dynamic and compartmentalized nature of the intracellular environment. This review proposes a systems pharmacology framework centered on subcellular pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic (Sub-PK/PD) profiling to predict and optimize intracellular combination therapies. Mechanistic and translational studies of intracellular drug disposition, host-pathogen metabolism, computational combination design, and biomimetic infection models were synthesized in a targeted narrative review. Particular attention was given to spatially resolved measurements, dual ribonucleic acid (RNA) sequencing, metabolic flux analysis, machine learning, and organ-on-a-chip platforms. Pathogen-containing vacuoles, phagolysosomes, the host cytosol, lipid-rich macrophages, and tissue lesions impose distinct barriers to drug ionization, accumulation, stability, and target engagement. Persistent infection also produces reciprocal metabolic rewiring: host pathways supply carbon, nitrogen, lipids, metals, and reducing equivalents, while bacterial stress programs alter growth and antibiotic susceptibility. Integrating these processes can reveal shared metabolic bottlenecks suitable for combinations of pathogen-directed and host-directed agents. Computational models can prioritize combinations, but their predictions require validation under physiologically realistic concentration-time profiles. Linking systems biology to localized Sub-PK/PD provides a practical roadmap for designing niche-specific regimens. Such regimens could improve clearance of persistent intracellular reservoirs, reduce ineffective exposure, and limit the emergence of antimicrobial resistance.

articles.title: Molecularly guided pharmacotherapy for obesity: emerging targets, clinical efficacy, and personalized therapeutic approaches.
articles.abstract: Obesity is a complex, chronic disease whose aetiology is complex and highly variable, and is linked to a network of neural, endocrine, adipose, genetic, epigenetic and metabolic pathways. This molecular complexity also drives significant differences in the clinical course of disease, drug sensitivity and weight regain, thus making standardized treatment, which is largely based on BMI and clinical empiricism, challenging. This narrative review explores the molecular mechanisms involved in obesity and the potential to apply the knowledge of molecular mechanisms to develop more personalized treatment strategies using advances in pharmacology. It focuses on hypothalamic appetite-satiety pathways, gut-brain hormonal communication, inflammation and metabolic dysfunction in adipose tissue, and known and novel drug targets. The review focuses on the evidence available on GLP-1 receptor agonism, GIP-GLP-1 co-agonism, multi-agonism with glucagon, signaling of amylin, melanocortin pathways, and novel central and peripheral targets. Studies have shown that some dual- and triple-receptor drugs are more effective at causing weight loss, and practitioners should consider tolerability, sustainability, cardiometabolic effects, and response when choosing drugs or drug combinations for patients. Inter-individual variability may be further explained by genetic, epigenetic, metabolic, and tissue-specific factors, which may help identify mechanisms of resistance. In conclusion, Inter-individual variability may be attributed to genetic, epigenetic, metabolic, and tissue-specific factors, and most suggested molecular or biomarker predictors have not yet proven sufficiently valid or useful for routine drug selection. Receptor-targeted drugs, including GLP-1 receptor agonists and GIP-GLP-1 co-agonists, are currently clinically actionable for patients with common obesity and available to specific patients with obesity, genotype-directed molecular therapeutic drugs are clinically actionable only for selected genetically defined types of obesity. However, the use of pharmacogenomic, biomarker, and multi-omics methods to guide the choice of anti-obesity drugs are still in their early stages of clinical investigation.

articles.title: CLDN18.2 in colorectal mucinous adenocarcinoma: a lineage-associated biomarker and emerging translational target.
articles.abstract: Colorectal mucinous adenocarcinoma (CMA) is a histologically and molecularly distinct subtype of colorectal cancer (CRC), marked by abundant extracellular mucin, a predilection for the proximal colon, and frequent overlap with deficient mismatch repair/high microsatellite instability (dMMR/MSI-H), BRAF V600E mutation, CpG island methylator phenotype-high (CIMP-high) status, and serrated pathway biology. Although immune checkpoint inhibitors and molecularly targeted therapies have expanded treatment options for selected patients with advanced CRC, treatment strategies tailored to the histologic phenotype, lineage programs, and microenvironmental architecture of CMA remain limited. CLDN18.2, the gastric isoform encoded by CLDN18, is now a clinically validated therapeutic target in gastric and gastroesophageal junction (GEJ) adenocarcinomas. Recent pathology-based studies suggest that CLDN18.2 expression is uncommon in unselected conventional colorectal adenocarcinoma but enriched in CMA, mucin-rich CRC, and tumors with gastric-type or foregut-like differentiation, particularly those arising in the proximal colon or harboring dMMR/MSI-H status or BRAF V600E mutation. This pattern suggests that CLDN18.2 in CMA is unlikely to be a classic oncogenic driver; instead, it is better viewed as a therapeutically accessible, lineage-associated membrane antigen. This review summarizes the biological rationale, expression data, companion diagnostic issues, therapeutic platforms, and translational barriers relevant to CLDN18.2 in CMA. We propose a framework centered on lineage reprogramming, antigen enrichment, assay standardization, and therapeutic translation. Current evidence supports CLDN18.2 as a candidate biomarker for biomarker-enriched investigation, not as an established therapeutic target in CMA. Future work should prioritize CMA-specific preclinical models, standardized membranous immunohistochemistry (IHC) scoring, and prospective trials that integrate CLDN18.2 expression with molecular subtype and tumor microenvironmental features.

articles.title: Rethinking Ayurvedic antibacterials: a mechanistic case for multi-target phytochemicals as adjuvants against antimicrobial resistance.
articles.abstract: Antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is now among the foremost threats to global health, and the pipeline of new antibiotics has not kept pace with it. A structural driver of resistance is often overlooked: the dominant "single molecule-single target" paradigm of antibiotic design imposes a well-defined selective pressure that bacteria can escape through a single mutation or acquired gene. This review reframes the antibacterial potential of Ayurvedic herbs around that problem. Rather than cataloguing herbs as candidate "natural antibiotics," we argue that their value lies in polypharmacology-the simultaneous action of structurally diverse secondary metabolites (flavonoids, tannins, saponins, phenolic acids and terpenoids) on multiple conserved bacterial targets, a combination against which stepwise resistance is evolutionarily improbable. We synthesise the mechanistic evidence for representative Ayurvedic plants including Calotropis procera, Azadirachta indica, Ocimum sanctum, the Acacia genus and Asparagus racemosus, organising it by bacterial target rather than by species: cell-wall biosynthesis, membrane integrity, and essential enzymes such as DNA gyrase and β-lactamase. We then examine two roles in which multi-target phytochemicals address failures of conventional therapy: the disruption of biofilms and quorum sensing, and synergy with existing antibiotics through efflux inhibition, β-lactamase suppression and extracellular-matrix degradation. Finally, we assess the translational barriers: reproducibility, heavy-metal contamination and the scarcity of clinical trials that currently confine most of this evidence to in vitro studies. We conclude that the most credible near-term contribution of Ayurvedic pharmacology to the AMR crisis is not as a replacement for antibiotics but as a source of multi-target adjuvants that restore and extend their efficacy.

articles.title: NRF2: sensing stress, shaping immunity - keeping inflammation quiet and antigens out of sight.
articles.abstract: The Cap 'n' Collar basic leucine zipper transcription factor NRF2 has been linked to inflammation almost since its identification as the master regulator of oxidative stress responses. Early studies demonstrated systemic inflammation and dysregulated immune responses following NRF2 loss. Initially, NRF2 was thought to regulate pro-inflammatory genes primarily through its antioxidant function, by binding to antioxidant response elements. However, studies by Kobayashi et al. revealed that, in LPS-treated murine macrophages, NRF2 binds to a non-ARE sequence near the Il6 and Il1b genes, where it regulates RNA polymerase II recruitment and represses pro-inflammatory gene transcription. More recent findings have further expanded the role of NRF2 in regulating immune and inflammatory responses by demonstrating that NRF2 suppresses transcription of the MHC class II transactivator (Ciita), a master regulator of major histocompatibility complex class II expression and antigen presentation. This article provides an overview of the historical evidence linking NRF2 to inflammatory conditions and discusses the emerging role of NRF2 in the transcriptional control of pro-inflammatory cytokines and Ciita. The molecular mechanisms through which NRF2 regulates Il6, Il1b, and Ciita remain incompletely understood and may involve yet-unidentified transcriptional co-regulators, which will be explored in this review.

articles.title: Comparing the analgesic effect of fluoxetine plus vitamin e with vitamin e alone on mastodynia due to fibrocystic breast disease: a randomized double-blind clinical trial.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Mastodynia is a common symptom in women with fibrocystic breast disease and can substantially impair quality of life. Although vitamin E is frequently used for symptom relief, the potential additional analgesic effect of fluoxetine remains unclear. This study aimed to compare the analgesic effect of fluoxetine plus vitamin E with that of vitamin E plus placebo in women with mastodynia associated with fibrocystic breast disease. METHODS: This double-blind, randomized clinical trial enrolled 78 women with mastodynia associated with fibrocystic breast disease who attended clinics affiliated with Shahrekord University of Medical Sciences, Shahrekord, Iran. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1) to receive either vitamin E (400 IU/day) plus fluoxetine (10 mg/day) or vitamin E (400 IU/day) plus placebo for 8 weeks. Randomization was computer-generated, allocation was concealed using identical medication packaging, and participants, investigators, and outcome assessors were blinded to treatment allocation. The primary outcome was breast pain intensity, assessed using the Visual Analog Scale (VAS) at baseline and at 1 and 2 months after treatment initiation. Secondary outcomes included breast heaviness, breast itching, and adverse events. Data were analyzed using repeated-measures analysis of variance and appropriate categorical tests. Seventy participants (35 per group) completed the study and were included in the analysis. RESULTS: Baseline demographic and clinical characteristics were comparable between the two groups. Repeated-measures analysis of variance demonstrated significant effects of treatment group (F (1,68) = 11.056, P = 0.001), time (F (2,136) = 164.321, P < 0.001), and the group-by-time interaction (F (2,136) = 60.996, P < 0.001) on breast pain intensity. No significant between-group differences were observed at baseline or after 1 month of treatment; however, after 2 months, breast pain intensity was significantly lower in the fluoxetine plus vitamin E group than in the vitamin E plus placebo group (P < 0.001). Breast heaviness was also significantly less frequent in the combination therapy group after 1 month (P = 0.009). Three participants in the fluoxetine group discontinued treatment because of adverse events, and no serious adverse events were reported in either group. CONCLUSIONS: The addition of fluoxetine to vitamin E improved breast pain after 8 weeks compared with vitamin E plus placebo in women with mastodynia associated with fibrocystic breast disease. These findings suggest that fluoxetine may be a useful adjunctive treatment; however, larger multicenter randomized trials with longer follow-up are needed to confirm its efficacy and safety. TRIAL REGISTRATION: Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (IRCT20200205046381N1), registered on February 28, 2020.

articles.title: The placental transfer of nirmatrelvir using the ex vivo human placental perfusion model.
articles.abstract: AIMS: Nirmatrelvir is an effective therapeutic option for COVID-19 infection and is often administered after symptom onset in pregnant individuals, but few data are available on the associated fetal exposure. The placental perfusion model evaluates maternal-fetal drug transfer across the human placenta and thus can determine fetal drug exposure. The objective of our study was to quantify the amount of nirmatrelvir transfer across the human placenta using the ex vivo placental perfusion model. METHODS: In a dual closed-closed perfusion of a single human placenta lobule, nirmatrelvir was added to the maternal circulation at its clinical concentration (2.21 μg/mL) or at 10 times this level (22.1 μg/mL). For each placenta studied, there was a 1-h perfusion control period followed by a 3-h exposure period. Samples of the perfusate were collected throughout the experiment to measure nirmatrelvir concentrations and placental viability markers. RESULTS: Perfusions conducted with nirmatrelvir at 2.21 μg/mL (n = 4) and 22.1 μg/mL (n = 5) concentrations showed a fetal-maternal concentration ratio (F:M) of 0.34 and 0.42, respectively, at 180 min. F:M was adjusted for nonplacental physiological factors, including binding of albumin and α-1-acid glycoprotein, and ionization. The adjusted F:M ranged from 0.26 to 0.35 for placentas perfused with 2.21 μg/mL and from 0.33 to 0.47 for placentas perfused with 22.1 μg/mL of nirmatrelvir. CONCLUSIONS: Nirmatrelvir readily crosses the term human placenta in a concentration-dependent manner. These transfer kinetics provide a foundation for future physiologically based pharmacokinetic modelling, supporting the development of personalized nirmatrelvir dosing strategies in pregnancy.

articles.title: Development and Temporal Validation of a Risk Prediction Model for Piperacillin/Tazobactam Induced Thrombocytopenia in Older Patients.
articles.abstract: BACKGROUND: Drug-induced immune thrombocytopenia (DITP) is a rare but potentially life-threatening adverse drug reaction, with evidence largely limited to case reports. Piperacillin-tazobactam (PTZ) appears to carry a relatively higher risk, particularly in older patients. This study aims to elucidate the clinical characteristics and risk factors associated with piperacillin-tazobactam (PTZ)-induced thrombocytopenia in older patients, to develop and validate a risk prediction model. METHODS: In this retrospective cohort study, we screened 5,454 older inpatients (≥60 years) treated with PTZ for pulmonary infections at Xiangya Hospital (2020-2022) for model development, with a separate 2024 cohort for temporal validation. After strict exclusion, 258 patients entered the model development phase (202 non-cases and 56 thrombocytopenia cases). Among the 56 cases, 40 were confirmed as PTZ-related and analyzed by multivariate logistic regression to identify independent risk factors, leaving 242 patients in the final development cohort. Model performance was evaluated using the separate temporal validation cohort (n=151) via receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analysis. RESULTS: PTZ-related thrombocytopenia occurred in 16.5% (40/242) of the development cohort. The independent risk factors identified included: baseline platelet count ≤150×10⁹/L (OR=8.065, 95% CI: 3.510-18.530), serum creatinine ≥80 μmol/L (OR=3.925, 95% CI: 1.752-8.797), aspartate aminotransferase ≥30 U/L (OR=3.154, 95% CI: 1.415-7.028), and hemoglobin ≤90 g/L (OR=3.172, 95% CI: 1.319-7.629). The prediction model achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.819 (95% CI: 0.753-0.885) in the development set and 0.713 (95% CI: 0.568-0.858) in the temporal validation set. CONCLUSION: A predictive model incorporating baseline platelet count, serum creatinine, aspartate aminotransferase, and hemoglobin demonstrated good discriminative performance for PTZ-induced thrombocytopenia in older patients, supporting its potential utility for individualized risk stratification.

articles.title: Cannabidiol prevents fear extinction deficits caused by single prolonged stress in rats: possible involvement of serotoninergic, cannabinoid, and nitric mechanisms.
articles.abstract: Post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) involves impaired extinction learning, autonomic and neuroendocrine dysregulation, and first-line selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) show limited efficacy. We investigated effects and mechanisms of cannabidiol (CBD) on fear deficits induced by the single prolonged stress (SPS) model in male Wistar rats. SPS sensitized conditioned fear, impaired extinction recall, enhanced cardiovascular reactivity to trauma-related cues, and produced a trend toward a biphasic corticosterone response. Repeated post-SPS paroxetine (an SSRI, 10 mg/kg, 7 days) prevented these behavioral deficits. Repeated CBD (5 and 10 mg/kg, 7 days) prevented extinction memory impairments, and these effects were attenuated by the 5-HT1A antagonist WAY-100635 and the CB1 antagonist AM281. In the prelimbic medial prefrontal cortex (PL-mPFC), SPS increased neuronal nitric oxide synthase (nNOS) phosphorylation after extinction recall, which repeated CBD normalized, an effect prevented by WAY-100635 and attenuated by AM281. A single post-SPS injection of the competitive and preferential nNOS inhibitor 7-nitroindazole (7-NI, 30 and 60 mg/kg), used as a pharmacological tool, also prevented fear sensitization and extinction deficits. A single dose of CBD was effective at 30 mg/kg, but not at 5 or 10 mg/kg, and reduced nNOS phosphorylation. Neither CBD regimen altered total nNOS, CB1, or 5-HT1A levels. Both compounds remained effective in a stress-restress paradigm with a forced swim trauma reminder, although neither normalized the SPS-induced increase in total nNOS. These findings indicate that CBD prevents SPS-induced extinction deficits through 5-HT1A- and CB1-dependent mechanisms, identify nNOS as a candidate downstream substrate, and support CBD as a multi-target candidate for PTSD treatment.

articles.title: Genetically predicted cocaine addiction vulnerability is associated with elevated GABAergic transmission in the central amygdala of drug-naïve rats.
articles.abstract: A central unresolved question in addiction neuroscience is whether the cellular differences that distinguish vulnerable from resilient individuals precede drug exposure or arise as its consequence. Because addiction-like phenotypes are conventionally assigned only after drug exposure, existing evidence cannot readily separate predisposition from neuroadaptation. Here we used RATTACA, a genome-wide prediction method developed for heterogeneous stock (HS) rats, to select drug-naïve rats with high or low genetically predicted cocaine addiction severity and characterized synaptic transmission by whole-cell recording before any drug exposure, in three independent cohorts. Rats with a high predicted addiction severity showed elevated spontaneous inhibitory postsynaptic current (sIPSC) frequency in the medial subdivision of the central amygdala (CeM), and sIPSC frequency scaled continuously with the predicted severity across rats. Amplitude and kinetics were unchanged, a pattern consistent with greater presynaptic GABAergic input. In separate cohorts, GABAergic transmission in the nucleus accumbens core (NAc core) and glutamatergic transmission in the CeM did not differ between groups, suggesting that, among the measures examined, the association was specific to CeM inhibitory transmission. Bath-applied cocaine reduced CeM sIPSC frequency by a similar proportion in both groups and increased CeM glutamatergic transmission. Because high-predicted rats started from a higher baseline, the absolute reduction in spontaneous inhibitory input was larger in these rats. Groups did not differ in locomotor activity. These findings identify elevated spontaneous GABAergic transmission in the CeM as a pre-existing correlate of polygenic cocaine addiction risk and show that genome-wide prediction can dissociate innate cellular predisposition from drug-induced adaptation.

articles.title: Kaempferol protects against the nephrotoxic changes induced by ifosfamide: Cross-talk between apoptosis, mitochondrial dysfunction, TXNIP-associated pyroptosis, and endoplasmic reticulum stress pathways.
articles.abstract: Ifosfamide is a chemotherapeutic agent that is widely used in the treatment of diverse groups of malignancies. Nevertheless, its clinical utility is constrained by the risk of overt nephrotoxicity. The objective of this study was to evaluate the possible protective effects of kaempferol at different doses in a rat model of ifosfamide-induced renal injury and to elucidate the underlying mechanisms. Using Wistar rats, the impact of kaempferol on renal functions, oxidative stress, pyroptotic markers, apoptosis, and endoplasmic reticulum stress markers was investigated, alongside histopathological assessment. Kaempferol produced a significant dose-dependent improvement in the renal functions, and strengthened antioxidant defenses in the renal tissues compared with ifosfamide-treated controls. Additionally, it attenuated the alterations in inflammatory responses, apoptosis, pyroptosis, and endoplasmic reticulum stress-related markers while ameliorating ifosfamide-induced structural damage in renal tissues, with the most pronounced effects observed at higher doses. In conclusion, kaempferol demonstrates promising potential in protecting against ifosfamide-elicited renal damage, warranting further mechanistic studies to clarify the molecular and cellular pathways that may be involved.

articles.title: Combined baicalein and the neocryptolepine derivative Z2 enhance anti-ovarian cancer efficacy by inhibiting the CDK4/6-Rb signaling pathway.
articles.abstract: Ovarian cancer is a highly aggressive gynecological malignancy with poor prognosis, creating an urgent need for novel therapeutic agents and rational combinatorial strategies. Herein, a panel of pre-synthesized neocryptolepine derivatives was subjected to biological screening. Derivative Z2 exerted potent anti-proliferative activity against SKOV3 and ES2 ovarian cancer cells (IC₅₀ = 1.91 ± 0.07 μM, 2.21 ± 0.11 μM), with low cytotoxicity in normal KGN cells. As monotherapy, Z2 suppressed cell migration, induced G0/G1-phase arrest and mitochondria-dependent apoptosis by elevating intracellular ROS and reducing mitochondrial membrane potential. Subsequently, CompuSyn analysis confirmed strong synergistic anti-tumor interactions between Z2 and baicalein. Compared with monotherapy, their combination further enhanced G0/G1 arrest, apoptosis and migration inhibition. Mechanistically, molecular docking predicted stable binding of both compounds to CDK4. Western blot and CDK4/CDK6 agonist (INK4C-IN-2) rescue assays performed in SKOV3 and ES2 cells demonstrated that Z2 baicalein co treatment inhibited the CDK4/6-Rb cascade, and reactivation of this pathway partially abrogated the synergistic antitumor effect, indicating the essential role of the CDK4/6-Rb axis. Furthermore, acute-toxicity assays validated the favorable in vivo safety of Z2 within certain doses. In ID8 syngeneic tumor-bearing mice, Z2-baicalein co-treatment markedly suppressed tumor growth without obvious organ toxicity. Collectively, Z2 is a promising anti-ovarian-cancer lead compound, and Z2-baicalein combination constitutes a feasible synergistic regimen targeting the CDK4/6-Rb signaling axis.

articles.title: Anthraquinone-enriched fraction of Rheum australe D. Don by Bioassay-guided fractionation and synergistic interaction with tetracycline against Bacterial pathogens.
